Vanadurgā
------------------------------------------
She is one of the several aspects of दुर्गा (See DURGĀ.) described in icono-graphical works. Her complexion is greenish like fresh grass. She has eight arms. In seven, she carries चक्र (discus), शङ्ख (conch), asi (sword), carma (shield), बाण (arrow), cāpa (bow) and śūla (spear). The eighth is showing the tarjanī मुद्रा (gesture of threat). She stands on the head of महिषासुर (buffalo-demon).
As the name indicates, her shrines are perhaps established in vanas or forests.

vānaprastha
(‘forest hermit’)
------------------------------------------
This is the third stage of life for a द्विज (the twice-born, a member of the first three castes). Vaikhānasa seems to have been the ancient name for a वानप्रस्थ.
Generally, a गृहस्थ (a होउसे-holder), around the age of 50 or 55, after the birth of grand-children, when the hair starts turning grey and the skin gets wrinkled, is expected to hand over the responsibilities of the family to his children and retire to the vana or forest. He may take his wife if she is willing to share his life of austerities or leave her with his sons.
If he had established the śrauta or the Vedic fires, he could carry the same with him to the forest also. Otherwise he could carry the gṛhya or domestic fire.
He was expected to perform some śrauta sacrifices like the दर्शपूर्णमास and the Cāturmāsyas.
He had the freedom to give up the śrauta fires and kindle a separate fire for certain limited rituals.
He had to live an austere life by not shaving the hair, growing a beard, subsisting on simple ड़ोओद् available in the forest like roots, vegetables and fruits or even by begging from other hermits. Eating once a day and occasional ड़स्तिन्ग् were emphasised.
Bathing thrice or twice a day, wearing a deerskin or coarse garments, performing the five daily sacrifices (See PAÑCAMAHĀ-YAJÑAS.), studying the वेदस् and observing continence were compulsory. He was expected to devote his मिन्द् in contemplation on God or ब्रह्मन्.
Some dharmaśāstra works describe four types of vānaprasthas.
Vānaprasthas who were suffering from severe old-age ailments or incurable diseases could commit religious सुइचिदे by महाप्रस्थान (walking unto death) or by entering a river or fire.
Though ब्राह्मणस् could take to सṁन्यास after वानप्रस्थ stage, it was denied to others.

Vanamālā
(‘garland of forest flowers’)
------------------------------------------
If विष्णु’s garland is known as वैजयन्ती, कृष्ण’s is called वनमाला. Since he spent his childhood days at गोकुल (a small village situated in a forest area) he loved to wear a garland (= mālā) of flowers available in a forest (= vana). They must be fresh flowers of all varieties with a large kadamba (Nauclea cadamba) flower in the centre.
